rows.evidence: Q1: Sections III-VI, Tables 1-4 - author compiles statewise secondary data for 14 Indian states at four time points (1972-73 to 1987-88) and runs own correlation and OLS regression analyses of irrigated area per thousand rural population against rural poverty and related variables.
rows.notes: The study concerns irrigation in general (gross irrigated area, irrigated area per rural population) and its statistical relationship with rural poverty, wages, foodgrain productivity and SDP. It contains nothing on drip or micro-irrigation, water consumption, or energy/electricity use of well extraction. No own result on the claimed technology or effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections III-VI, Tables 1-4 - own regression/correlation analysis of statewise secondary data on irrigation and rural poverty across 14 Indian states.
rows.notes: The study does show that irrigated area (general irrigation, all types) is positively associated with foodgrain productivity (PFG) and foodgrain production per head across states (Table 1), but this is about irrigation in aggregate, not drip or micro-irrigation versus flood irrigation. No evidence on drip crop yield.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections III-VI, Tables 1-4 - own regression/correlation analysis of statewise secondary data on irrigation and rural poverty across 14 Indian states.
rows.notes: The study does not mention drip irrigation, weeds or weed control at all. It is a macro-level analysis of aggregate irrigation and rural poverty.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections III-VI, Tables 1-4 - own regression/correlation analysis of statewise secondary data on irrigation and rural poverty across 14 Indian states.
rows.notes: The study does not mention drip irrigation, soil erosion or any soil variable. It is a macro-level analysis of aggregate irrigation and rural poverty.

notes: Full text appears complete (one paragraph is duplicated in the scan). The study is Narayanamoorthy (2001) 'Irrigation and Rural Poverty Nexus: A Statewise Analysis', an econometric analysis of general irrigation coverage and rural poverty in India; it contains no material on drip or micro-irrigation, so all four claim rows are technology mismatches. The review may have intended a different Narayanamoorthy 2001 paper on drip irrigation.
